title: Body & health
goal: Name parts of the body, say what hurts and what illness you have, understand a doctor's advice and say what someone should do.
intro:
Telugu talks about pain and illness as things that **happen to you**: *నాకు జ్వరం వచ్చింది* (a fever came to me), *నాకు తలనొప్పిగా ఉంది* (to me it is headache-ly). The person affected is in the dative case, just like *నాకు కావాలి* and *నాకు ఇష్టం*.

You'll also learn the very useful ending **-ఆలి** (-āli), 'must, should', which works the same for every person.

phrases.en: I've had a fever for two days.
How should I take this medicine?

grammar.title: Aches and illnesses: the experiencer in the dative
grammar.body:
Feelings and illnesses happen *to* you, so the person is in the **dative** (నాకు, మీకు, అతనికి ...):
• **నాకు X గా ఉంది** for a state you feel: *నాకు తలనొప్పిగా ఉంది* (I have a headache), *నాకు నీరసంగా ఉంది* (I feel weak).
• **నాకు X వచ్చింది** (X came to me) for illnesses you catch: *జ్వరం వచ్చింది*. For a cold, Telugu says *జలుబు చేసింది* (the cold did [it] to me).
• For a specific body part, use the possessive: *నా కాలు నొప్పిగా ఉంది* (my leg hurts), or the dative of the body part: *నా చేతికి దెబ్బ తగిలింది* (an injury touched my hand = I hurt my hand).

examples.en: The little girl has caught a cold.

grammar.title: Should and must: -ఆలి, and 'should not': -కూడదు
grammar.body:
Add **-ఆలి** (-āli) to the verb stem for 'must / should / have to'. It is the **same for all persons**: *నేను వెళ్ళాలి* (I must go), *మీరు వెళ్ళాలి* (you must go).
తిను → తినాలి · తాగు → తాగాలి · వెళ్ళు → వెళ్ళాలి · చేయు → చేయాలి · రా → రావాలి · తీసుకో → తీసుకోవాలి

'Should not / must not' is **-అకూడదు** (-akūḍadu): *తినకూడదు* (shouldn't eat). For gentle advice, use the conditional + **మంచిది**: *విశ్రాంతి తీసుకుంటే మంచిది* (it's better if you rest).

examples.en: You should go to the doctor.
You must take this medicine three times a day.
It's good to drink plenty of water.

dialogue.title: At the clinic
dialogue.setting: Suresh visits a family doctor with a fever.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.en: Come in, sit down. What's the matter?

lines.speaker: Suresh
lines.en: Fever and a headache for two days.

lines.speaker: Suresh
lines.native: కొంచెం దగ్గు ఉంది. ఒంట్లో చాలా నీరసంగా ఉంది.
lines.roman: konchem daggu undi. oṇṭlō chālā nīrasaṅgā undi.
lines.en: A slight cough. I feel very weak.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.en: Open your mouth... Your throat is red.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: లేదు, మామూలు వైరల్ జ్వరం. ఈ మందులు రోజుకి మూడుసార్లు వేసుకోండి.
lines.roman: lēdu, māmūlu vairal jvaram. ī mandulu rōjuki mūḍusārlu vēsukōṇḍi.
lines.en: No, it's an ordinary viral fever. Take these medicines three times a day.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: తర్వాత. బాగా విశ్రాంతి తీసుకోవాలి, వేడి నీళ్ళు తాగాలి.
lines.roman: tarvāta. bāgā vishrānti tīsukōvāli, vēḍi nīḷḷu tāgāli.
lines.en: After. You must rest well and drink warm water.

culture: Home remedies are a first resort: turmeric milk (*పసుపు పాలు*) for a cough, *చారు* (rasam) with pepper and garlic for a cold, and *మజ్జిగ* (buttermilk) to cool the body in summer. Many people distinguish 'heat' and 'cold' foods (*వేడి చేసింది*, 'it has caused heat', is a common complaint). Pharmacies (*మందుల షాపు*) are everywhere and pharmacists often give advice directly.
